Educational synthesis for curriculum design (not legal/security advice).

  • Context engineering and tool-description quality dominate output quality.
  • Eval design builds taste; golden sets and judge calibration matter.
  • Model routing + fallback chains beat defaulting to one frontier model.
  • Permissions become security perimeter once agents run tools unattended.

🧠 Practice Bank — LLM internals

Dense MCQ practice over 80 facts · 80 questions · tap each to reveal the answer and one-line explanation.

Q1. Tokenization
  1. A. Compresses weights only
  2. B. Maps raw text into discrete tokens for the model
  3. C. Maps pixels to vectors
  4. D. Stores KV cache on disk

✅ Answer: B — Maps raw text into discrete tokens for the model
💡 Tokenizers convert text into discrete units the model processes.

Q2. BPE
  1. A. Uses fixed 1-char tokens only
  2. B. Merges frequent character pairs into tokens iteratively
  3. C. Splits only on whitespace
  4. D. Deletes rare words

✅ Answer: B — Merges frequent character pairs into tokens iteratively
💡 BPE builds vocabulary by greedily merging frequent pairs.

Q3. Self-attention
  1. A. Freezes all embeddings
  2. B. Lets each token weight information from other tokens
  3. C. Only looks at the next word
  4. D. Removes position signals

✅ Answer: B — Lets each token weight information from other tokens
💡 Self-attention uses queries, keys, and values to mix context.

Q4. Multi-head attention
  1. A. Disables residual paths
  2. B. Runs several attention subspaces in parallel
  3. C. Uses one head always
  4. D. Replaces softmax with max

✅ Answer: B — Runs several attention subspaces in parallel
💡 Multiple heads capture different relation types.

Q5. Transformer block
  1. A. Only does recurrence
  2. B. Stacks attention, feed-forward, residuals, and norms
  3. C. Only does convolution
  4. D. Only does pooling

✅ Answer: B — Stacks attention, feed-forward, residuals, and norms
💡 A transformer layer combines attention and MLP with residuals.

Q6. KV cache
  1. A. Caches tokenizer rules only
  2. B. Stores past keys and values to speed autoregressive decode
  3. C. Stores training labels
  4. D. Deletes old tokens always

✅ Answer: B — Stores past keys and values to speed autoregressive decode
💡 KV cache avoids recomputing attention over prior tokens.

Q7. Context window
  1. A. Training dataset size only
  2. B. Maximum tokens a model can condition on in one pass
  3. C. GPU RAM only
  4. D. Number of API keys

✅ Answer: B — Maximum tokens a model can condition on in one pass
💡 Context length bounds history and documents per call.

Q8. RoPE
  1. A. Removes position entirely
  2. B. Encodes relative position via rotations in attention
  3. C. Adds random noise only
  4. D. Stores absolute line numbers only

✅ Answer: B — Encodes relative position via rotations in attention
💡 RoPE rotates query/key vectors by position.

Q9. GPTQ
  1. A. Trains architecture from scratch
  2. B. Post-training weight quantization optimized for GPUs
  3. C. Changes only the tokenizer
  4. D. Deletes the attention layer

✅ Answer: B — Post-training weight quantization optimized for GPUs
💡 GPTQ quantizes weights after training for cheaper inference.

Q10. AWQ
  1. A. Quantizes only embeddings
  2. B. Activation-aware weight quantization preserving salient channels
  3. C. Always uses 32-bit only
  4. D. Removes MoE routers

✅ Answer: B — Activation-aware weight quantization preserving salient channels
💡 AWQ protects important weights using activation stats.

Q11. GGUF
  1. A. A RAG vector index only
  2. B. llama.cpp-friendly quantized model file format
  3. C. A cloud-only API schema
  4. D. A TTS codec

✅ Answer: B — llama.cpp-friendly quantized model file format
💡 GGUF packages quantized weights for local serving.

Q12. MoE
  1. A. Disables attention
  2. B. Routes tokens to sparse expert FFNs to scale capacity
  3. C. Uses one dense FFN only
  4. D. Removes batching

✅ Answer: B — Routes tokens to sparse expert FFNs to scale capacity
💡 MoE activates a subset of experts per token.

Q13. RLHF
  1. A. Only freezes embeddings
  2. B. Aligns models using human preference feedback signals
  3. C. Only unsupervised clustering
  4. D. Only shrinks context

✅ Answer: B — Aligns models using human preference feedback signals
💡 RLHF steers behavior toward preferred outputs.

Q14. DPO
  1. A. Removes all fine-tuning
  2. B. Direct preference optimization without a separate reward model stage
  3. C. Requires only unlabeled images
  4. D. Forces greedy decoding only

✅ Answer: B — Direct preference optimization without a separate reward model stage
💡 DPO optimizes on preferred vs rejected pairs directly.

Q15. LoRA
  1. A. Tokenizer-only updates
  2. B. Low-rank adapters on frozen base weights for efficient fine-tunes
  3. C. Full-rank rewrite of every weight
  4. D. Quantization of prompts only

✅ Answer: B — Low-rank adapters on frozen base weights for efficient fine-tunes
💡 LoRA adds small trainable matrices while freezing the base.

Q16. QLoRA
  1. A. Deletes adapters after each step
  2. B. LoRA on a quantized base model to cut memory further
  3. C. Always needs multi-node clusters
  4. D. Uses no rank parameter

✅ Answer: B — LoRA on a quantized base model to cut memory further
💡 QLoRA pairs 4-bit bases with LoRA adapters.

Q17. Temperature
  1. A. Sets batch size
  2. B. Scales logits before sampling; higher means more random
  3. C. Changes learning rate only
  4. D. Fixes context length

✅ Answer: B — Scales logits before sampling; higher means more random
💡 Temperature controls sampling randomness.

Q18. Top-p
  1. A. Drops the KV cache
  2. B. Samples from smallest token set with cumulative probability at least p
  3. C. Always picks argmax only
  4. D. Sets embedding dim

✅ Answer: B — Samples from smallest token set with cumulative probability at least p
💡 Nucleus sampling truncates the distribution tail.

Q19. Perplexity
  1. A. Measures GPU utilization only
  2. B. Exponential of average negative log-likelihood; lower is better fit
  3. C. Always equals accuracy
  4. D. Counts unique users

✅ Answer: B — Exponential of average negative log-likelihood; lower is better fit
💡 Perplexity summarizes model surprise on text.

Q20. Hallucination
  1. A. A tokenizer merge rule
  2. B. Confident generation not grounded in evidence or facts
  3. C. A type of embedding only
  4. D. A CUDA kernel

✅ Answer: B — Confident generation not grounded in evidence or facts
💡 Hallucinations invent unsupported content.

Q21. Pretraining
  1. A. Only tool-schema design
  2. B. Next-token learning on massive unlabeled corpora
  3. C. Only preference ranking
  4. D. Only UI theming

✅ Answer: B — Next-token learning on massive unlabeled corpora
💡 Pretraining builds general language competence.

Q22. Instruction tuning
  1. A. Only builds FAISS indexes
  2. B. Fine-tunes on instruction-response pairs for chat utility
  3. C. Only quantizes weights
  4. D. Only records traces

✅ Answer: B — Fine-tunes on instruction-response pairs for chat utility
💡 Instruction data teaches task following.

Q23. Causal mask
  1. A. Removes all padding
  2. B. Prevents attending to future tokens in left-to-right decode
  3. C. Forces bidirectional always
  4. D. Locks temperature to zero

✅ Answer: B — Prevents attending to future tokens in left-to-right decode
💡 Causal masking blocks future leakage.

Q24. FlashAttention
  1. A. A TTS vocoder
  2. B. Memory-efficient tiled attention reducing HBM traffic
  3. C. A RAG reranker only
  4. D. A vector DB

✅ Answer: B — Memory-efficient tiled attention reducing HBM traffic
💡 FlashAttention improves attention IO efficiency.

Q25. Speculative decoding
  1. A. Removes sampling
  2. B. Drafts with a small model then verifies with a large model
  3. C. Always doubles context
  4. D. Disables KV cache

✅ Answer: B — Drafts with a small model then verifies with a large model
💡 Speculative decoding can raise tokens per second.

Q26. GQA
  1. A. Removes positional encodings
  2. B. Shares KV heads across query groups to shrink KV cache
  3. C. Always uses full MHA only
  4. D. Forces MoE off

✅ Answer: B — Shares KV heads across query groups to shrink KV cache
💡 Grouped-query attention reduces decode memory.

Q27. Softmax in attention
  1. A. Shuffles tokens randomly
  2. B. Normalizes scores into a probability distribution
  3. C. Clips gradients only
  4. D. Compresses GGUF files

✅ Answer: B — Normalizes scores into a probability distribution
💡 Softmax turns scores into weights that sum to one.

Q28. Residual connection
  1. A. Forces zero init always
  2. B. Adds sublayer input to output to ease gradient flow
  3. C. Removes skip paths
  4. D. Deletes attention scores

✅ Answer: B — Adds sublayer input to output to ease gradient flow
💡 Residuals help deep stacks train.

Q29. Feed-forward block
  1. A. Only does STT
  2. B. Applies position-wise nonlinear transform after attention
  3. C. Only does cross-document retrieval
  4. D. Only does canary deploys

✅ Answer: B — Applies position-wise nonlinear transform after attention
💡 FFN is major per-token compute.

Q30. LayerNorm/RMSNorm
  1. A. Only caches HTML
  2. B. Stabilizes activations across features
  3. C. Only shuffles batches
  4. D. Only sets top-k

✅ Answer: B — Stabilizes activations across features
💡 Normalization stabilizes deep transformers.

Q31. Mixed precision
  1. A. Removes gradients always
  2. B. Uses fp16/bf16 tensors to speed training and inference
  3. C. Forces int8 tokenizer only
  4. D. Disables CUDA

✅ Answer: B — Uses fp16/bf16 tensors to speed training and inference
💡 Lower precision often raises throughput.

Q32. Gradient checkpointing
  1. A. Only affects tokenizer
  2. B. Recomputes activations backward to save memory
  3. C. Always increases peak VRAM
  4. D. Only affects TTS

✅ Answer: B — Recomputes activations backward to save memory
💡 Checkpointing trades compute for memory.

Q33. Scaling laws
  1. A. Only apply to STT
  2. B. Relate loss to compute, data, and parameters roughly as power laws
  3. C. Say size never matters
  4. D. Only apply to vector DBs

✅ Answer: B — Relate loss to compute, data, and parameters roughly as power laws
💡 Scaling laws guide pretraining budgets.

Q34. Tokenizer fertility
  1. A. Number of experts only
  2. B. Average tokens per word; higher fertility lengthens sequences
  3. C. GPU temperature only
  4. D. Eval hit rate only

✅ Answer: B — Average tokens per word; higher fertility lengthens sequences
💡 Fertility affects cost and effective context.

Q35. Stop sequences
  1. A. Only used in RAG chunking
  2. B. End generation when a configured string pattern appears
  3. C. Always ignored by models
  4. D. Only used in STT VAD

✅ Answer: B — End generation when a configured string pattern appears
💡 Stop sequences bound tool and format outputs.

Q36. Logit bias
  1. A. Changes embedding files on disk
  2. B. Adds offsets to specific token logits before sampling
  3. C. Rewrites the training set
  4. D. Deletes the system prompt

✅ Answer: B — Adds offsets to specific token logits before sampling
💡 Logit bias can ban or encourage tokens.

Q37. Repetition penalty
  1. A. Replaces retrieval
  2. B. Down-weights already generated tokens to reduce loops
  3. C. Always improves factuality
  4. D. Sets chunk size

✅ Answer: B — Down-weights already generated tokens to reduce loops
💡 Repetition control is a decode heuristic.

Q38. System prompt
  1. A. A FAISS index path only
  2. B. High-priority instruction context steering model behavior
  3. C. A CUDA driver version
  4. D. A GGUF quant flag only

✅ Answer: B — High-priority instruction context steering model behavior
💡 System prompts set role and constraints.

Q39. Few-shot prompting
  1. A. Always needs RLHF
  2. B. Provides worked examples in-context to shape the task
  3. C. Always fine-tunes weights
  4. D. Always needs MoE

✅ Answer: B — Provides worked examples in-context to shape the task
💡 In-context examples teach patterns without weight updates.

Q40. Chain-of-thought
  1. A. Only works with no text
  2. B. Encourages intermediate reasoning steps before the final answer
  3. C. Disables all reasoning text
  4. D. Replaces evaluation

✅ Answer: B — Encourages intermediate reasoning steps before the final answer
💡 Step-by-step traces can help hard reasoning.

Q41. Prefill vs decode
  1. A. Prefill only runs on CPU always
  2. B. Prefill processes the prompt in parallel; decode emits tokens sequentially
  3. C. They are identical stages
  4. D. Decode never uses KV cache

✅ Answer: B — Prefill processes the prompt in parallel; decode emits tokens sequentially
💡 Latency budgets must separate both stages.

Q42. Continuous batching
  1. A. Disables streaming
  2. B. Dynamically batches decode requests to raise GPU utilization
  3. C. Only batches offline ETL
  4. D. Forces single-user only

✅ Answer: B — Dynamically batches decode requests to raise GPU utilization
💡 Serving stacks batch in-flight generations.

Q43. PagedAttention
  1. A. Only for STT buffers
  2. B. Manages KV cache in non-contiguous blocks like virtual memory
  3. C. Pages only HTML
  4. D. Only for CSS

✅ Answer: B — Manages KV cache in non-contiguous blocks like virtual memory
💡 Paged KV packs concurrent sequences better.

Q44. Constrained decoding
  1. A. Only quantizes adapters
  2. B. Forces outputs to obey a grammar or JSON schema
  3. C. Removes all constraints
  4. D. Only sets theme colors

✅ Answer: B — Forces outputs to obey a grammar or JSON schema
💡 Structured outputs reduce tool parse failures.

Q45. Distillation
  1. A. Only copies HTML
  2. B. Trains a smaller student to match a larger teacher behavior
  3. C. Always enlarges the student
  4. D. Only copies FAISS

✅ Answer: B — Trains a smaller student to match a larger teacher behavior
💡 Distillation compresses capability into cheaper models.

Q46. Catastrophic forgetting
  1. A. Only affects disk format
  2. B. Fine-tuning on new tasks can erase prior skills without care
  3. C. Always improves every skill
  4. D. Only affects CSS

✅ Answer: B — Fine-tuning on new tasks can erase prior skills without care
💡 Adapters and data mix reduce forgetting.

Q47. SFT
  1. A. Only preference pairs always
  2. B. Supervised fine-tuning on labeled instruction and response demos
  3. C. Only unsupervised clustering
  4. D. Only quantization

✅ Answer: B — Supervised fine-tuning on labeled instruction and response demos
💡 SFT is a common first alignment stage.

Q48. Attention sink
  1. A. Only affects FAISS
  2. B. Some early tokens disproportionately absorb attention mass
  3. C. Only a water metaphor
  4. D. Only affects TTS pitch

✅ Answer: B — Some early tokens disproportionately absorb attention mass
💡 Long-context research studies attention mass concentration.

Q49. Model card
  1. A. A chunk size only
  2. B. Documents intended use, limits, evals, and safety notes
  3. C. A GPU SKU only
  4. D. A theme CSS file only

✅ Answer: B — Documents intended use, limits, evals, and safety notes
💡 Model cards communicate use boundaries.

Q50. Inference engine
  1. A. Only a slideshow
  2. B. Runtime that loads weights and serves generation efficiently
  3. C. Only a design doc
  4. D. Only a marketing PDF

✅ Answer: B — Runtime that loads weights and serves generation efficiently
💡 vLLM, llama.cpp, and TensorRT-LLM are engines.

Q51. Autoregressive generation
  1. A. Never uses context
  2. B. Produces tokens one-by-one conditioned on prior tokens
  3. C. Generates all tokens fully parallel always
  4. D. Only embeds documents

✅ Answer: B — Produces tokens one-by-one conditioned on prior tokens
💡 Most LLMs decode autoregressively.

Q52. Decoder-only LM
  1. A. Cannot generate text
  2. B. Uses causal self-attention for generative language modeling
  3. C. Is always bidirectional
  4. D. Is only a vector DB

✅ Answer: B — Uses causal self-attention for generative language modeling
💡 GPT-style models are decoder-only.

Q53. Embedding table
  1. A. A STT waveform only
  2. B. Lookup matrix mapping token IDs to vectors
  3. C. A SQL join only
  4. D. A canary flag only

✅ Answer: B — Lookup matrix mapping token IDs to vectors
💡 Embedding tables are large edge parameter blocks.

Q54. Vocabulary size
  1. A. Number of users only
  2. B. Number of distinct tokens the model can emit or consume
  3. C. Number of GPUs only
  4. D. Number of CSS files only

✅ Answer: B — Number of distinct tokens the model can emit or consume
💡 Vocab size trades compression vs table size.

Q55. Soft prompt tuning
  1. A. Only changes GGUF magic
  2. B. Learns continuous prompt vectors instead of full fine-tunes
  3. C. Always rewrites all weights
  4. D. Only changes STT sample rate

✅ Answer: B — Learns continuous prompt vectors instead of full fine-tunes
💡 Prompt tuning is a light adaptation method.

Q56. Adapter layers
  1. A. Only affects CSS shell
  2. B. Inserts small modules between frozen base layers
  3. C. Deletes residual paths
  4. D. Only affects resource IDs

✅ Answer: B — Inserts small modules between frozen base layers
💡 Adapters specialize without full retrain.

Q57. Rejection sampling
  1. A. Disables all filters
  2. B. Generates many candidates and keeps those that pass filters
  3. C. Always accepts first token
  4. D. Only used for image resize

✅ Answer: B — Generates many candidates and keeps those that pass filters
💡 Best-of-N can raise quality at higher cost.

Q58. Overfitting in fine-tunes
  1. A. Never happens with LoRA
  2. B. Memorizes narrow demos and fails to generalize
  3. C. Always improves OOD
  4. D. Only affects STT

✅ Answer: B — Memorizes narrow demos and fails to generalize
💡 Holdout evals combat overfit.

Q59. YaRN/NTK scaling
  1. A. Only shrink context
  2. B. Techniques to extend context beyond original training length
  3. C. Always free and perfect
  4. D. Only change vocab size

✅ Answer: B — Techniques to extend context beyond original training length
💡 Length extension needs careful eval.

Q60. Beam search
  1. A. Deletes the FFN
  2. B. Keeps multiple partial sequences searching higher joint probability
  3. C. Samples only one random token
  4. D. Quantizes only biases

✅ Answer: B — Keeps multiple partial sequences searching higher joint probability
💡 Beam search trades compute for search depth.

Q61. Top-k sampling
  1. A. Deletes KV cache
  2. B. Samples only from the k highest-probability tokens
  3. C. Always samples full vocab
  4. D. Sets learning rate

✅ Answer: B — Samples only from the k highest-probability tokens
💡 Top-k is a simple truncation sampler.

Q62. Weight tying
  1. A. Freezes only the router
  2. B. Shares input embedding and output projection weights
  3. C. Duplicates all layers
  4. D. Quantizes only KV

✅ Answer: B — Shares input embedding and output projection weights
💡 Tying can reduce parameter count.

Q63. Cross-entropy loss
  1. A. Only measures cost
  2. B. Standard next-token training objective against true labels
  3. C. Only measures latency
  4. D. Only measures citations

✅ Answer: B — Standard next-token training objective against true labels
💡 Cross-entropy pushes mass onto the correct token.

Q64. Teacher forcing
  1. A. Only used in TTS eval
  2. B. Training feeds gold previous tokens rather than model samples
  3. C. Always uses model samples only
  4. D. Only used in canary deploys

✅ Answer: B — Training feeds gold previous tokens rather than model samples
💡 Teacher forcing stabilizes LM training.

Q65. Entropy of predictions
  1. A. Equals context length
  2. B. High entropy means higher next-token uncertainty
  3. C. Always means more factual
  4. D. Equals GPU count

✅ Answer: B — High entropy means higher next-token uncertainty
💡 Entropy helps detect ambiguity.

Q66. Sliding window attention
  1. A. Deletes embeddings
  2. B. Limits attention to a local window for long sequences
  3. C. Forces full global always
  4. D. Disables sampling

✅ Answer: B — Limits attention to a local window for long sequences
💡 Local windows trade reach for efficiency.

Q67. Numerics-stable softmax
  1. A. Only fixed by more CSS
  2. B. Subtracts max logit before exp for numerical stability
  3. C. Never needed in practice
  4. D. Only fixed by more chunks

✅ Answer: B — Subtracts max logit before exp for numerical stability
💡 Stable softmax prevents overflow.

Q68. Context stuffing failure
  1. A. Always reduces cost
  2. B. Huge unprioritized text dilutes attention and hurts answers
  3. C. Always improves retrieval
  4. D. Always raises MRR

✅ Answer: B — Huge unprioritized text dilutes attention and hurts answers
💡 Curate evidence; more tokens are not always better.

Q69. Tool-aware training
  1. A. Only does image crop
  2. B. Teaches models when and how to call external tools
  3. C. Removes all APIs
  4. D. Only does CSS minify

✅ Answer: B — Teaches models when and how to call external tools
💡 Tool use extends models beyond pure text.

Q70. Inference batch size
  1. A. Chunk overlap only
  2. B. Number of sequences processed together at serve time
  3. C. Number of training epochs only
  4. D. Number of themes only

✅ Answer: B — Number of sequences processed together at serve time
💡 Batch size trades latency, throughput, and memory.

Q71. Special tokens
  1. A. Always embeddings of images
  2. B. Reserved tokens for BOS/EOS/pad/tool boundaries and roles
  3. C. Always plain English words
  4. D. Always SQL keys

✅ Answer: B — Reserved tokens for BOS/EOS/pad/tool boundaries and roles
💡 Special tokens structure chat protocols.

Q72. Absolute vs relative position
  1. A. Only absolute works for all tasks
  2. B. Absolute indexes positions; relative encodes pairwise distances
  3. C. Positions never matter
  4. D. Only relative works for images always

✅ Answer: B — Absolute indexes positions; relative encodes pairwise distances
💡 Position schemes affect length generalization.

Q73. Curriculum learning
  1. A. Deletes hard examples only
  2. B. Orders training examples from easier to harder patterns
  3. C. Randomizes labels always
  4. D. Only reorders CSS

✅ Answer: B — Orders training examples from easier to harder patterns
💡 Curriculum can stabilize complex skill acquisition.

Q74. Undertraining
  1. A. Only means high temperature
  2. B. Stops before the model absorbs enough signal from data
  3. C. Always means too much data
  4. D. Only means large top-p

✅ Answer: B — Stops before the model absorbs enough signal from data
💡 Learning curves reveal undertraining.

Q75. Detokenization artifacts
  1. A. Only affects vector DBs
  2. B. Bad decode can insert spaces or break code formatting
  3. C. Never affects code
  4. D. Only affects themes

✅ Answer: B — Bad decode can insert spaces or break code formatting
💡 Round-trip tests catch detokenization bugs.

Q76. Logprobs
  1. A. Disk SMART errors
  2. B. Per-token log probabilities useful for scoring and calibration
  3. C. GPU fan curves
  4. D. DNS TTL values

✅ Answer: B — Per-token log probabilities useful for scoring and calibration
💡 Logprobs support confidence and constrained decode.

Q77. Activation sparsity
  1. A. Only tokenizer is sparse
  2. B. Only a subset of parameters activate per token in sparse models
  3. C. All weights always fire equally
  4. D. Only CSS is sparse

✅ Answer: B — Only a subset of parameters activate per token in sparse models
💡 Sparsity can raise capacity without full dense cost.

Q78. Bidirectional encoder
  1. A. Never uses attention
  2. B. Sees full sequence both directions for understanding tasks
  3. C. Only sees future tokens
  4. D. Only for TTS

✅ Answer: B — Sees full sequence both directions for understanding tasks
💡 Encoders suit embedding tasks.

Q79. Cross-attention
  1. A. Always disabled in multimodal
  2. B. Attends from one sequence into another sequence
  3. C. Always self-only
  4. D. Only for CSS

✅ Answer: B — Attends from one sequence into another sequence
💡 Cross-attention links modalities or encoder-decoder paths.

Q80. Parameter count
  1. A. Equals latency always
  2. B. Total learnable weights; rough capacity proxy not quality guarantee
  3. C. Equals always quality
  4. D. Equals safety always

✅ Answer: B — Total learnable weights; rough capacity proxy not quality guarantee
💡 Size helps but data and training matter too.

📚 Practice Bank — RAG & retrieval

Dense MCQ practice over 77 facts · 77 questions · tap each to reveal the answer and one-line explanation.

Q81. RAG
  1. A. Only changes temperature
  2. B. Retrieves external evidence then conditions generation on it
  3. C. Only fine-tunes weights always
  4. D. Only does STT

✅ Answer: B — Retrieves external evidence then conditions generation on it
💡 RAG grounds answers in fetched documents.

Q82. Chunking
  1. A. Only tokenizes the query
  2. B. Splits documents into retrievable passages of bounded size
  3. C. Always keeps whole books as one vector
  4. D. Only quantizes the model

✅ Answer: B — Splits documents into retrievable passages of bounded size
💡 Chunk boundaries dominate retrieval quality.

Q83. Chunk overlap
  1. A. Only used in TTS
  2. B. Repeats boundary text across adjacent chunks to reduce split loss
  3. C. Always zero for best quality
  4. D. Only used in CSS

✅ Answer: B — Repeats boundary text across adjacent chunks to reduce split loss
💡 Overlap helps questions straddling sections.

Q84. Semantic chunking
  1. A. Deletes embeddings
  2. B. Splits on meaning boundaries rather than fixed counts only
  3. C. Always uses 1-token chunks
  4. D. Disables hybrid search

✅ Answer: B — Splits on meaning boundaries rather than fixed counts only
💡 Structure-aware splits often beat naive windows.

Q85. Embeddings
  1. A. GPU fan curves
  2. B. Dense vectors that place similar text near each other
  3. C. Sparse bag-of-words only always
  4. D. CSS color tokens

✅ Answer: B — Dense vectors that place similar text near each other
💡 Embeddings enable nearest-neighbor semantic search.

Q86. bge embeddings
  1. A. A CUDA driver
  2. B. Strong open embedding family often used for retrieval
  3. C. A TTS vocoder family
  4. D. A theme pack

✅ Answer: B — Strong open embedding family often used for retrieval
💡 bge models are common RAG embedding baselines.

Q87. mpnet embeddings
  1. A. Only for STT
  2. B. Sentence-transformer style encoders for semantic similarity
  3. C. Only for image generation
  4. D. Only for quantization

✅ Answer: B — Sentence-transformer style encoders for semantic similarity
💡 mpnet models are classic embedding baselines.

Q88. Vector database
  1. A. Only stores CSS
  2. B. Stores embeddings and supports similarity search at scale
  3. C. Only stores raw WAV
  4. D. Only stores GPU kernels

✅ Answer: B — Stores embeddings and supports similarity search at scale
💡 Vector DBs index embeddings for fast kNN.

Q89. FAISS
  1. A. A LoRA trainer only

  4. D. A browser theme

Q90. Chroma
  1. A. A SIP trunk

  1. A. Disables reranking always

  1. A. A TTS codec

  1. A. Always equals cost

  1. A. Measures CSS size only
  2. B. Averages one over rank of the first relevant result

Q98. nDCG
  1. A. Only token count

  1. A. Speed only

  1. A. Equals temperature

  1. A. Only measures cost
  2. B. Relevant evidence needed was actually retrieved
  3. C. Always equals precision

  1. A. Always raise temperature

Q104. Metadata filters
  1. A. Only change temperature
  2. B. Constrain retrieval by source, date, ACL, or type
  3. C. Only change embedding dim

  1. A. Only filters by language

Q107. HyDE
  1. A. Always disables BM25

  3. C. Always returns only 1 token

  1. A. Only cite temperature
  2. B. Force answers to cite supporting chunk IDs
  3. C. Never cite sources

  1. A. Only matters for TTS

  1. A. Only for audio
  2. B. Removes near-duplicate chunks that crowd top-k
  3. C. Always keeps all duplicates
  4. D. Only for CSS

Q112. ANN search
  1. A. Never used in vector DBs
  2. B. Approximate nearest neighbor trades exactness for speed
  3. C. Always exact only
  4. D. Only for STT

Q113. HNSW
  1. A. A LoRA rank only
  2. B. Graph-based ANN index common in vector stores
  3. C. A TTS spectrogram

Q114. Product quantization
  1. A. Deletes all indexes

  3. C. Always raises quality free
  4. D. Only for images always

  1. A. Never normalize whitespace

Q116. Multi-vector documents
  1. A. Never helps long docs
  2. B. Represent one document with multiple vectors
  3. C. Always one float only

Q117. Golden set for RAG
  1. A. No labels needed ever
  2. B. Labeled query-evidence-answer cases for regression
  3. C. Random traffic only

  1. A. Skip metrics

  1. A. Always prefer SEO spam

Q121. Temporal queries
  1. A. Always use oldest only

  3. C. Time never matters

  1. A. Never re-query

  1. A. Never helps multi-hop

  1. A. Only measure one demo average

  1. A. Never version embeddings

  1. A. No metrics

  3. C. Only positives
  4. D. Ignore

✅ Answer: B — State what not to do carefully
💡 Negatives help but need tests.

Q374. Persona prompting
  1. A. Conflicting personas
  2. B. Assign a role to shape style and priorities
  3. C. No persona
  4. D. Persona equals truth

✅ Answer: B — Assign a role to shape style and priorities
💡 Personas steer style not facts.

Q375. Self-check prompt
  1. A. Always trust first draft
  2. B. Ask model to verify constraints before final answer
  3. C. Never self-check
  4. D. No verify

✅ Answer: B — Ask model to verify constraints before final answer
💡 Self-checks catch format errors.

Q376. Decomposition
  1. A. No steps
  2. B. Break hard tasks into ordered substeps
  3. C. One giant ask always
  4. D. Parallel chaos

✅ Answer: B — Break hard tasks into ordered substeps
💡 Decomposition improves hard tasks.

Q377. Scratchpad prompting
  1. A. Show all secrets
  2. B. Allow hidden intermediate work then final clean answer
  3. C. No intermediate
  4. D. No structure

✅ Answer: B — Allow hidden intermediate work then final clean answer
💡 Separate work and user answer.

Q378. Retrieval-augmented prompt
  1. A. Invent sources
  2. B. Insert evidence blocks with cite instructions
  3. C. No evidence
  4. D. Ignore docs

✅ Answer: B — Insert evidence blocks with cite instructions
💡 Ground prompts in retrieved text.

Q379. Tool-use instructions
  1. A. No schemas
  2. B. When and how to call tools with schemas
  3. C. Vague tool prose
  4. D. Call everything always

✅ Answer: B — When and how to call tools with schemas
💡 Clear tool policy raises accuracy.

Q380. Length control
  1. A. No budget
  2. B. Budget words or tokens for answers
  3. C. Unlimited ramble
  4. D. Always max tokens

✅ Answer: B — Budget words or tokens for answers
💡 Length control improves UX and cost.

Q381. Temperature for tasks
  1. A. Max temp always
  2. B. Lower temp for factual; higher for creative
  3. C. One temp all tasks
  4. D. Temp equals truth

✅ Answer: B — Lower temp for factual; higher for creative
💡 Match sampling to task risk.

Q382. Prompt versioning
  1. A. No versions
  2. B. Name and track prompt versions like code
  3. C. Edit silently
  4. D. No diffs

✅ Answer: B — Name and track prompt versions like code
💡 Versions enable RTMA on prompts.

Q383. Prompt injection
  1. A. Always blocked free
  2. B. User or doc content tries to override system rules
  3. C. Impossible
  4. D. Ignore

✅ Answer: B — User or doc content tries to override system rules
💡 Defend with boundaries and filters.

Q384. Jailbreak resistance
  1. A. Assume safe
  2. B. Stay within policy under adversarial prompts
  3. C. No tests
  4. D. Delete fails

✅ Answer: B — Stay within policy under adversarial prompts
💡 Suites of jailbreaks belong in CI.

Q385. Context prioritization
  1. A. Bury rules
  2. B. Put critical constraints where models attend reliably
  3. C. Random order
  4. D. Duplicate contradictions

✅ Answer: B — Put critical constraints where models attend reliably
💡 Order and repetition are design tools.

Q386. Ambiguity handling
  1. A. Never clarify
  2. B. Ask clarifying questions when needed
  3. C. Always guess
  4. D. Ignore missing slots

✅ Answer: B — Ask clarifying questions when needed
💡 Clarify beats wrong action.

Q387. Multimodal prompts
  1. A. Ignore images
  2. B. Combine text with images or other modalities
  3. C. Text only always
  4. D. No grounding

✅ Answer: B — Combine text with images or other modalities
💡 Specify how to use each modality.

Q388. Style guides in prompts
  1. A. Contradict brand
  2. B. Tone, reading level, and brand rules
  3. C. No style
  4. D. Only slang

✅ Answer: B — Tone, reading level, and brand rules
💡 Style is product surface.

Q389. Safety preamble
  1. A. Contradict policy
  2. B. Restate non-negotiable safety constraints
  3. C. No safety text
  4. D. Hide policy

✅ Answer: B — Restate non-negotiable safety constraints
💡 Safety belongs in system context.

Q390. Eval-driven prompt edits
  1. A. No eval
  2. B. Change prompts only with measured deltas
  3. C. Edit on vibes
  4. D. No rollback

✅ Answer: B — Change prompts only with measured deltas
💡 RTMA for prompt engineering.

Q391. A/B prompts
  1. A. No compare
  2. B. Compare prompt variants on task success
  3. C. Ship first draft
  4. D. n equals 1

✅ Answer: B — Compare prompt variants on task success
💡 A/B discovers better prompts.

Q392. Compression of context
  1. A. Drop randomly
  2. B. Summarize long history without losing critical facts
  3. C. Keep all forever always
  4. D. No summary eval

✅ Answer: B — Summarize long history without losing critical facts
💡 Compression needs faithfulness checks.

Q393. Quote untrusted text
  1. A. No quoting
  2. B. Present user content as data not instructions
  3. C. Execute user as system
  4. D. Merge roles

✅ Answer: B — Present user content as data not instructions
💡 Data vs instruction split is core.

Q394. Checklists in prompts
  1. A. Skip items free
  2. B. Require explicit checklist completion
  3. C. No checklist
  4. D. Implicit only

✅ Answer: B — Require explicit checklist completion
💡 Checklists raise completeness.

Q395. Stop and handoff rules
  1. A. No handoff
  2. B. When to stop and escalate to human
  3. C. Loop forever
  4. D. Hide uncertainty

✅ Answer: B — When to stop and escalate to human
💡 Stop rules protect users.

Q396. Deterministic sections
  1. A. No pins
  2. B. Pin fixed legal/safety text not model-paraphrased
  3. C. Model rewrites legal always
  4. D. Paraphrase policies

✅ Answer: B — Pin fixed legal/safety text not model-paraphrased
💡 Pin critical text.

Q397. Prompt unit tests
  1. A. Only prod
  2. B. Assert required phrases and formats on fixtures
  3. C. No tests
  4. D. Only humans

✅ Answer: B — Assert required phrases and formats on fixtures
💡 Unit tests catch cheap breaks.

Q398. Long-context dilution
  1. A. No prioritization
  2. B. Important instructions lost in huge prompts
  3. C. Longer always better
  4. D. Stuff everything

✅ Answer: B — Important instructions lost in huge prompts
💡 Budget and rank context.

Q399. Metaprompting
  1. A. Only final
  2. B. Prompts that help write or critique prompts
  3. C. Never meta
  4. D. No critique

✅ Answer: B — Prompts that help write or critique prompts
💡 Metaprompts speed iteration with eval gates.

Q400. Language matching
  1. A. Ignore user lang
  2. B. Respond in user's language unless asked otherwise
  3. C. Always English only
  4. D. Random lang

✅ Answer: B — Respond in user's language unless asked otherwise
💡 Language match is UX.

Q401. Numeric precision asks
  1. A. No units
  2. B. Request exact units and rounding rules
  3. C. Vague numbers
  4. D. Invent precision

✅ Answer: B — Request exact units and rounding rules
💡 Precision specs reduce ambiguity.

Q402. Table output prompts
  1. A. No headers
  2. B. Ask for markdown tables with fixed columns
  3. C. Free mess
  4. D. Inconsistent cols

✅ Answer: B — Ask for markdown tables with fixed columns
💡 Tables help comparison tasks.

Q403. JSON only mode
  1. A. Trailing commentary
  2. B. Require pure JSON with no prose wrappers
  3. C. JSON plus jokes
  4. D. Invalid JSON OK

✅ Answer: B — Require pure JSON with no prose wrappers
💡 Strict JSON for tools.

Q404. Repair loop
  1. A. No repair
  2. B. If parse fails, re-ask with error details
  3. C. Fail hard silent
  4. D. Infinite repair no cap

✅ Answer: B — If parse fails, re-ask with error details
💡 Bounded repair improves reliability.

Q405. Citation prompts
  1. A. Invent cites
  2. B. Require quotes and source IDs for claims
  3. C. No cites
  4. D. Cites optional always

✅ Answer: B — Require quotes and source IDs for claims
💡 Citations enable audit.

Q406. Uncertainty language
  1. A. Never hedge
  2. B. Express confidence bands when appropriate
  3. C. Always certain
  4. D. Fake precision

✅ Answer: B — Express confidence bands when appropriate
💡 Calibrated language builds trust.

Q407. Domain glossaries
  1. A. No glossary
  2. B. Provide term definitions in prompt context
  3. C. Assume jargon known
  4. D. Contradict defs

✅ Answer: B — Provide term definitions in prompt context
💡 Glossaries stabilize terminology.

Q408. Time anchoring
  1. A. Always current free
  2. B. State as-of dates for time-sensitive answers
  3. C. Ignore time
  4. D. No dates

✅ Answer: B — State as-of dates for time-sensitive answers
💡 Time anchors reduce stale claims.

Q409. Counterexample asks
  1. A. No edges
  2. B. Request failure cases and edge conditions
  3. C. Happy path only
  4. D. Ignore falsifiers

✅ Answer: B — Request failure cases and edge conditions
💡 Campus teach-back style.

Q410. RTMA in prompts
  1. A. Only theory
  2. B. Ask for run, trace, metric, artifact in student tasks
  3. C. No proof
  4. D. No artifacts

✅ Answer: B — Ask for run, trace, metric, artifact in student tasks
💡 Learn while building, prove as you go.

Q411. Prompt budget tokens
  1. A. Always max
  2. B. Count tokens before send; trim low-value text
  3. C. Ignore counts
  4. D. OOM free

✅ Answer: B — Count tokens before send; trim low-value text
💡 Token budgets are real money.

Q412. Duplicate instruction harm
  1. A. No audit
  2. B. Contradictory repeated rules confuse models
  3. C. Duplicate freely contradict
  4. D. Mess OK

✅ Answer: B — Contradictory repeated rules confuse models
💡 Audit for contradictions.

Q413. Template variables
  1. A. No escape
  2. B. Safe substitution of user fields into templates
  3. C. String concat unsafe
  4. D. Inject raw

✅ Answer: B — Safe substitution of user fields into templates
💡 Treat templates like code.

Q414. Localization of prompts
  1. A. Machine translate no eval
  2. B. Translate and re-eval prompts per locale
  3. C. One locale only
  4. D. Ignore culture

✅ Answer: B — Translate and re-eval prompts per locale
💡 Locales need their own gates.

Q415. Secret non-inclusion
  1. A. Log secrets
  2. B. Never put API keys in prompts or logs
  3. C. Keys in prompts fine
  4. D. Share keys in few-shot

✅ Answer: B — Never put API keys in prompts or logs
💡 Secrets stay in secret stores.

Q416. Prompt lint
  1. A. Only human memory
  2. B. Static checks for missing sections and risks
  3. C. No lint
  4. D. Skip

✅ Answer: B — Static checks for missing sections and risks
💡 Lint cheaply prevents footguns.

Q417. Canonical system prompt
  1. A. Many forks
  2. B. Single source of truth for system text
  3. C. Copy-paste drift
  4. D. No source

✅ Answer: B — Single source of truth for system text
💡 DRY system prompts.

Q418. Feature flags for prompts
  1. A. No flags
  2. B. Toggle prompt sections with flags and evals
  3. C. Edit prod only
  4. D. Big bang

✅ Answer: B — Toggle prompt sections with flags and evals
💡 Flags enable canaries.

Q419. User preference memory prompts
  1. A. No consent
  2. B. Inject remembered prefs carefully with consent
  3. C. Silent memory always
  4. D. Stale prefs forever

✅ Answer: B — Inject remembered prefs carefully with consent
💡 Memory needs policy.

Q420. Critique then revise
  1. A. No critique
  2. B. Generate, critique, revise within one session
  3. C. First draft ship
  4. D. Infinite revise

✅ Answer: B — Generate, critique, revise within one session
💡 Bounded critique raises quality.

Q421. Tool failure instructions
  1. A. Hallucinate results
  2. B. What to do when tools error
  3. C. Ignore errors
  4. D. Crash

✅ Answer: B — What to do when tools error
💡 Error policies belong in prompts.

Q422. Empty evidence instructions
  1. A. Guess confidently
  2. B. What to say when retrieval is empty
  3. C. Invent
  4. D. No policy

✅ Answer: B — What to say when retrieval is empty
💡 Fail closed when empty.

Q423. Math process prompts
  1. A. No steps
  2. B. Require step-by-step with final boxed answer
  3. C. Answer only always
  4. D. Hide work

✅ Answer: B — Require step-by-step with final boxed answer
💡 Process helps verification.

Q424. Code generation prompts
  1. A. No tests
  2. B. Specify language, tests, and constraints
  3. C. Vague code ask
  4. D. Any lang

✅ Answer: B — Specify language, tests, and constraints
💡 Constraints reduce junk code.

Q425. Security coding prompts
  1. A. Allow eval raw
  2. B. Forbid dangerous APIs and require safe defaults
  3. C. Ignore secure coding
  4. D. No warnings

✅ Answer: B — Forbid dangerous APIs and require safe defaults
💡 Secure-by-default prompts.

Q426. Educational teach-back
  1. A. No teach-back
  2. B. Ask learner to explain rule, exception, example, falsifier
  3. C. Only multiple choice
  4. D. Memorize only

✅ Answer: B — Ask learner to explain rule, exception, example, falsifier
💡 Campus pattern for mastery.

Q427. Prompt canary strings
  1. A. Leak OK
  2. B. Detect if system prompt leaked in output
  3. C. No canaries
  4. D. Ignore

✅ Answer: B — Detect if system prompt leaked in output
💡 Canaries detect leakage.

Q428. Minimal viable prompt
  1. A. No baseline
  2. B. Start simple; add complexity only when evals demand
  3. C. Max complexity first
  4. D. Kitchen sink

✅ Answer: B — Start simple; add complexity only when evals demand
💡 Complexity is a cost.

Q429. Prompt ownership
  1. A. Everyone none
  2. B. Named owner for each production prompt
  3. C. Orphan prompts
  4. D. No review

✅ Answer: B — Named owner for each production prompt
💡 Ownership prevents drift.

Q430. Changelog for prompts
  1. A. No why
  2. B. Record why each prompt change happened
  3. C. Silent edits
  4. D. No link to metrics

✅ Answer: B — Record why each prompt change happened
💡 Changelogs complete RTMA.

Q431. Regression prompts
  1. A. Only new
  2. B. Keep historical hard cases as fixtures
  3. C. Delete hard cases
  4. D. No history

✅ Answer: B — Keep historical hard cases as fixtures
💡 Hard cases are treasure.

Q432. Cross-model prompts
  1. A. No retune
  2. B. Prompts may need retuning per model family
  3. C. One prompt all models perfect
  4. D. Ignore families

✅ Answer: B — Prompts may need retuning per model family
💡 Portability is tested not assumed.

Q433. Instruction hierarchy
  1. A. No hierarchy
  2. B. System > developer > user > tool data priority
  3. C. User always wins
  4. D. Tool data is system

✅ Answer: B — System > developer > user > tool data priority
💡 Hierarchy is a safety design.

Audience paths

Pick a rail. Ignore the rest (for now).

①

A · Beginner

D00 → RTMA → D01/D05 → golden slice labs → resource atlas “Local Lab”.

②

B · Domain expert

RTMA ↔ your incident grammar → agents D09 → evals D11 → domain braid.

③

C · Engineer

D01 + D07 + D09 + D11 + D13 · read lab source · ship scorecards.

🪄

D · Hermes track

D10 fully · approval gates · coach patterns · never YOLO unattended high privilege.

🎙️

E · Voice/UC

D12 + sibling UC free pack · latency budgets · human handoff.

🦾

F · Future/robotics

D14 foresight · VLA/world models · safety first · sim before real.

Evidence grammar

Run · Trace · Metric · Artifact

AI twin of UC LICC. Falsifier first. If you cannot show these four, you do not yet know the lesson.

▶️

Run

Exact command, notebook, Hermes task, or lab script executed.

🧵

Trace

Request IDs, logs, tool-call chain, timeline of events.

📏

Metric

Latency, tokens, cost, pass rate, error rate, approval lag.

📦

Artifact

File you can reopen: JSON, report, checklist, scrubbed screenshot.

⚡

Falsifier

What observation would kill “the model is smart enough”?

🛡️

Perimeter

Permissions are perimeter when agents run tools. No unattended YOLO.
